newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian deputy PM denies sex crime allegations.
newsitem.headline: Belgian deputy PM denies sex crime allegations.

text.p: Belgian Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo said on Monday he was the subject of a judicial investigation, following press allegations that he had indulged in sex with minors.

Di Rupo, who denies the allegations, said in a statement the public prosecutor's office in Brussels had lodged a request with the Belgian parliament that he be charged -- a first step towards lifting his immunity from prosecution.
The weekend allegations that he and a francophone regional minister were involved in paedophilia were a further shock to Belgians, already reeling from child sex and political murder scandals.
The new scandals affected Belgian financial markets, causing concern about government stability and weighing on the franc.
Lifting Di Rupo's parliamentary immunity would give him the chance to view the dossier against him, something that he has said he wants.
In his statement, he said the request would allow him to tackle the issue head-on so that, "I hope, this confusion, these mix-ups and fabrications can be stopped. That is essential."
"I wish to reaffirm that I have never had anything at all to do with paedophilia. No action in my private life has ever harmed anybody," he said.

The president of the Belgian parliament, Raymond Langendries, told the Belga news agency earlier that he had called a meeting of party leaders on Tuesday to discuss a file he had received on a government minister. He gave no details.
Constitutional experts said any decision to lift Di Rupo's immunity -- which would have to be taken by a full session of parliament -- would not necessarily force him to resign.

Jean-Pierre Grafe, a minister in the Walloon government who was named by Flemish newspapers on Monday alongside Di Rupo as being involved in sex with minors, also denied the allegations although francophone community leaders were to meet on Tuesday.
Di Rupo, who is also in charge of Belgium's fight against paedophile porn on the Internet, accused his political opponents of trying to stir up trouble.
"What is disgusting from some members of the opposition is that they are trying to use this in a political way," he told RTBF television.
A spokesman for the Brussels public prosecutor's office said: "The prosecutor general has begun work on a dossier in which two names of two ministers appear." He gave no details.
The sex allegations were not the only issues causing a stir in the heart of Belgium's coalition government on Monday.

Agriculture Minister Karel Pinxten was accused by the deputy director general of a semi-independent body fighting white-collar crime in the public sector of tax evasion and influence peddling -- charges he refuted.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, called on to clear the air over Di Rupo's position in the cabinet, remained silent on the topic on Monday. He nevertheless felt obliged to issue a statement denying a separate press report that he too had been involved in influence peddling.

Belgian politicians say they are facing a witch hunt reminiscent of the McCarthy years in the United States of the 1950s when a rumour of an affinity to communism was enough to disgrace any public figure.
Analysts say there is a widespread lack of confidence, not only in politics but also in Belgium's law and order system.

Papers publishing front-page reports on fresh scandals say it is their public duty and part of a catharsis the country needs after recent revelations of paedophile murder and allegations of political power-peddling and legal laxity.
The analysts said the government was not yet threatened by the clear-out of corruption begun some years ago.

The drive gained fresh impetus this summer by allegations of high-level cover-ups which emerged after four girls were found murdered and an investigation into the 1991 murder of a Socialist politician was re-opened.

A catalogue of police bungling and rivalry between different teams of investigators was unveiled along with revelations of judicial dithering that highlighted the role of politics in the promotion of magistrates.
